# Reader development results

## First two-machine benchmark (October 23, 2026)

The replicated-tree owner reader answers a warm 10M query in 3 to 10 ms at p50, against 2.7 to 4.4 seconds for today's single-process reader, and reaches slightly higher recall at the same beam. Recall@10 tops out at 0.924 in this sweep (beam 256, rerank 10), short of the 0.95 target, so the next sweep needs wider beams.

### What ran

Both runs use the 10M fixture (`gen-303030`, prefix `sha256/epoch31-reader35-10m-resumed`), the frozen development queries, exact top-100 references, and the two r6i.16xlarge machines in window `window-reader-dev-1792780638`. Readers are pinned to one hardware thread on each of 28 physical cores.

- **Untouched baseline** (`runs/baseline-untouched-10m`): commit `46affe999`, binary `baseline-46affe999c72`. Today's single-process reader on the coordinator, 100 queries one at a time, two configurations. It has no cache, so every query fetches its posting lists from S3 one after another.
- **Owner reader** (`runs/owners-2m-sweep1`): commit `cdc549d20`, binary `owners-cdc549d20be7`. The coordinator navigates the whole tree, scans owner 1's leaves and sends owner 2's leaves to the peer's scan server. All 1,000 queries, seven configurations, a parallel cold pass that fills caches, then a warm pass one query at a time.

### Recall and warm latency

| Configuration | Baseline recall@10 | Baseline p50 | Owner recall@10 | Owner p50 | Owner p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| beam 32, rerank 10 | 0.733 | 2,738 ms | 0.775 | 3.11 ms | 4.53 ms |
| beam 64, rerank 10 | 0.803 | 4,355 ms | 0.839 | 4.26 ms | 6.10 ms |
| beam 128, rerank 0 | | | 0.698 | 6.35 ms | 9.11 ms |
| beam 128, rerank 4 | | | 0.883 | 6.40 ms | 9.74 ms |
| beam 128, rerank 10 | | | 0.890 | 6.46 ms | 9.39 ms |
| beam 128, rerank 20 | | | 0.890 | 6.49 ms | 9.69 ms |
| beam 256, rerank 10 | | | 0.924 | 10.02 ms | 16.21 ms |

Owner recall is higher at the same beam because each owner reranks its own best `k × rerank`, so a query that reaches both owners reranks up to twice as many candidates. Rerank beyond 4 adds almost nothing at beam 128; recall is limited by which leaves the walk reaches.

### Where warm time goes (beam 128, rerank 10, medians)

| Step | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Local navigation on the query machine | 0.77 ms |
| Owner 1 scan on the query machine (51 leaves, 77K vectors) | 2.1 ms |
| Owner 2 scan on the peer (77 leaves, 115K vectors) | 3.7 ms |
| Owner 2 request overhead: encode, network, queue, decode | 1.3 ms |
| Whole query | 6.5 ms |

The remote owner sets latency: the local scan runs alongside the remote request and finishes first. Within each owner, the 1-bit scan is 85% of owner time (about 28 ns per vector on one thread); candidate selection is 10% and rerank 3%. Owner 2 scans 1.5 times as many leaves as owner 1, so this subtree placement concentrates these queries' work on the peer. 989 of 1,000 queries reach both owners.

### Data per warm query (beam 128, rerank 10, means)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Posting bytes scanned (IDs and 1-bit codes) | 21.8 MB |
| Cold-equivalent bytes: posting objects plus rerank vector pages | 22.9 MB |
| Machine-to-machine bytes (request and reply) | 10.5 KB |
| Posting fetches in the warm pass | 0 (maximum over all queries) |
| Peak extra heap on the query machine (p50) | 1.7 MB |
| Peak extra heap on the peer (p50) | 2.6 MB |
| CPU per query: query machine / peer (p50) | 3.7 ms / 3.7 ms |

The query machine's posting cache holds 594 MB after the sweep, which is all of owner 1's leaves. Opening the reader takes 2.8 s for routing metadata and 25 s for the one-time corpus hash; the saved receipt skips that hash on later opens.

### Caveats

- **One process per reader.** There is no A/A run yet, so run-to-run noise is unmeasured.
- **Not a matched comparison.** The baseline covers 100 queries and the owner reader 1,000, and the baseline's latency is almost entirely S3 fetches.
- **Cold-pass latencies are not cold-query measurements.** Queries ran 32 at a time and shared caches.
- **Same-recall comparison pending.** Owner and baseline recall differ at the same beam, so the speedup at equal recall still needs a matched curve.

### Next steps suggested by these numbers

- Sweep wider beams (384 to 1,024) to reach recall@10 of 0.95, and find the cheapest rerank that keeps it.
- Speed up the 1-bit scan, which dominates owner time: batch or parallelize leaves within a request, and check the scan kernel's per-vector cost.
- Measure the cost of the remote path with the all-local run, and look at the 1.3 ms request overhead.
- Run an A/A pair to set the noise floor before judging smaller changes.

## Second round: wide beams, noise floor and the remote path (October 23, 2026)

Recall@10 reaches the 0.95 target at beam 512 with rerank 10: 0.952 at 19.3 ms p50 and 27.6 ms p99 on two machines. Run-to-run noise is about 0.5% of total latency, and every query returns identical IDs across processes. Scanning both owners in one process returns identical results but is 25% to 49% slower at wide beams, because it scans the two owners one after the other.

### What ran

All three processes use binary `owners-cdc549d20be7` (commit `cdc549d20`), the 10M fixture, all 1,000 development queries and `configs/sweep2.json`, with a parallel cold pass and then a warm pass one query at a time.

- **A/A pair** (`runs/owners-2m-sweep2-aa`): two separate two-machine processes, each with a freshly restarted peer scan server.
- **All-local** (`runs/owners-local-sweep2`): one process on the coordinator that scans both owners itself, with the same per-owner shortlists.

### Recall and warm latency, two machines

| Configuration | Recall@10 | p50 | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| beam 128, rerank 10 | 0.890 | 6.48 ms | 9.49 ms |
| beam 384, rerank 4 | 0.935 | 14.46 ms | 22.34 ms |
| beam 384, rerank 10 | 0.944 | 14.50 ms | 22.39 ms |
| beam 512, rerank 4 | 0.943 | 19.18 ms | 27.79 ms |
| beam 512, rerank 10 | 0.952 | 19.33 ms | 27.57 ms |
| beam 768, rerank 10 | 0.967 | 27.11 ms | 39.36 ms |
| beam 1,024, rerank 10 | 0.975 | 34.69 ms | 48.28 ms |

Latency grows almost linearly with beam, because the beam sets the number of leaves scanned. At wide beams rerank matters more than at beam 128: moving from rerank 4 to 10 adds 0.009 recall at beam 512 for almost no latency.

### Noise floor

The two A/A processes differ by 0.1% to 0.3% in total warm latency per configuration, with 95% intervals within about ±0.5%. One configuration (beam 768) shows a 0.33% difference whose interval excludes zero, so a small difference between processes exists. Changes smaller than about 1% therefore need repeated processes to judge. Recall and returned IDs are identical in every query across the two processes and the all-local run.

### Where time goes, and the cost of the remote path (medians)

| Configuration | Two-machine p50 | Navigation | Owner 1 scan (local) | Owner 2 scan (peer) | Request overhead | All-local p50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| beam 128, rerank 10 | 6.48 ms | 0.75 ms | 2.05 ms | 3.62 ms | 1.30 ms | 6.06 ms |
| beam 384, rerank 10 | 14.51 ms | 0.77 ms | 6.37 ms | 10.56 ms | 1.37 ms | 18.76 ms |
| beam 512, rerank 10 | 19.33 ms | 0.79 ms | 9.15 ms | 15.39 ms | 1.45 ms | 25.26 ms |
| beam 768, rerank 10 | 27.12 ms | 0.84 ms | 16.08 ms | 22.31 ms | 1.55 ms | 39.25 ms |
| beam 1,024, rerank 10 | 34.70 ms | 0.86 ms | 21.90 ms | 29.09 ms | 1.67 ms | 52.29 ms |

Two-machine latency is close to navigation plus owner 2's scan plus request overhead, because owner 2 is always the slower owner and the local scan finishes first. The request overhead (encode, network, server queue and decode) is 1.3 to 1.7 ms and grows slowly with the number of leaves sent.

The all-local run scans owner 1 and then owner 2 on one thread, so its latency is close to navigation plus both scans. Its gap to two machines measures parallelism across owners, not the cost of the network. A one-machine reader that scanned both owners in parallel would land near navigation plus the slower scan, roughly 16 ms at beam 512, so the remote path itself costs about 1.5 ms plus the effect of the uneven split.

### Placement and data per query (two machines, means unless marked)

| Configuration | Leaves owner 1 / owner 2 (median) | Cold-equivalent bytes | Machine-to-machine bytes | Peak extra heap, query machine / peer (median) | CPU per query, both machines (median) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| beam 128, rerank 10 | 51 / 77 | 24.0 MB | 10.5 KB | 1.7 MB / 2.6 MB | 7.4 ms |
| beam 512, rerank 10 | 216 / 296 | 92.4 MB | 15.1 KB | 6.8 MB / 9.8 MB | 26.6 ms |
| beam 1,024, rerank 10 | 450 / 574 | 183.6 MB | 20.9 KB | 13.8 MB / 18.9 MB | 53.5 ms |

- **Owner 2 does the most work.** It scans 1.3 to 1.5 times as many leaves as owner 1 for these queries, although each owner holds half the leaves, so subtree placement sets the critical path.
- **A cold query would be expensive.** At the recall target it would fetch about 92 MB of posting objects, about 512 objects of 180 KB each. Warm queries fetch nothing.
- **The heap peak is the candidate list.** It grows with vectors scanned, at about 16 bytes per candidate before selection.
- **CPU per query roughly equals latency summed over owners.** Each owner scans on one thread.
- **The all-local cache ends at 1.2 GB**, every leaf of both owners. Its open took 4.6 s and skipped the corpus hash through the saved receipt.

### Suggested next changes, ranked by expected effect at the recall target

1. **Scan a request's leaves in parallel within each owner.** The 1-bit scan is about 85% of owner time and runs on one thread, so this attacks the 15 ms critical path directly. Judge it on latency and CPU per query together.
2. **Keep only the best `k × rerank` candidates while scanning**, with a bounded heap instead of one list of every scored vector. This removes the 7 to 19 MB heap peak and the selection step.
3. **Balance scan work between owners.** Owner 2's larger share sets latency. This is the placement experiment in CURRENT-PLAN.md, measured against these per-owner leaf counts.
4. **Reduce request overhead.** It is 1.5 ms at the recall target; its parts (JSON encoding of leaf IDs, server queueing, connection reuse) are not yet broken down.

### What ran

The 10M index was re-saved from its finished writer checkpoint (`rows-10000000-after-placement`), so the tree is the one the earlier rounds used. The save used writer `writer-v2-41878daf1277` with `--save-vector-store`. It writes saved format v2: exact leaf centroids live in posting objects, the writer persists each parent's packed child arrays, and each owner's full vectors are stored as an Arrow blockfile keyed by leaf and posting position. The generation is `gen-303030` under prefix `sha256/epoch31-reader36-10m-v2c`; its descriptor and storage config are in `rebuilds/v2-10m-c/`. The save took 251 s, including about 30 GB of vector blockfiles. A fresh reader validated every node, all 10M posting codes, every packed child code, and every stored vector against the hashed corpus, bit for bit. The vector check took 900 s of the 1,053 s validation, because it fetches posting lists one at a time.

The benchmark binary is `reader-v2-e3ad811b5604` (commit `e3ad811b5`). It adds leaf scans on a 16-thread pool per owner, bounded per-chunk shortlists, and the per-level and optimal recall diagnostics. All 1,000 development queries ran with the seven `sweep2` configurations. Three processes ran: an A/A pair reranking from the vector stores, and one reranking from the local corpus copies.

### Results

- **Results are unchanged.** Recall is identical to round two in every configuration, and every query returns identical IDs across both A/A processes, the corpus run, and the round-two runs on the v1 index.
- **Warm latency at the recall target falls 3.3×.** Beam 512 with rerank 10 gives recall@10 of 0.952 at 5.84 ms p50 and 7.07 ms p99, against 19.33 ms and 27.57 ms in round two. Across configurations the B/A latency ratio against round two is 0.20 to 0.69. The widest beams gain most, since the parallel scan removes per-leaf serial time: beam 1,024 runs at 7.13 ms against 34.69 ms.
- **Scan cost per vector falls from about 28 ns to 4 to 7 ns.** CPU per query rises slightly in total. At beam 512 the query machine and peer use 15.0 and 17.4 ms of CPU, against 26.6 ms for both in round two.
- **Request overhead and navigation are now a large share.** At beam 512 the peer scans in 3.0 ms, but its request takes 4.35 ms, so 1.36 ms is encoding, network, queueing and decoding. Navigation takes 0.74 ms. Together they are about 36% of the 5.84 ms.
- **Recall is limited by which leaves the walk reaches, not by scoring.** Optimal recall is 1.0 at every beam, so the reached number of leaves could hold every true neighbor. Leaf reach is 0.9527 at beam 512, and final recall is 0.9523, so 1-bit scoring and rerank lose almost nothing. Levels 1 and 2 keep every node; all the loss is in choosing 512 of 6,905 leaves by 4-bit centroid score.
- **Vector-store rerank costs about 0.45 ms per query warm.** The peer's rerank takes 0.56 ms from the store against 0.06 ms from the mapped corpus at beam 512, and the query is 9% slower (5.84 ms against 5.36 ms). The store path pays for a runtime hop, a fresh blockfile reader per call and a copy per vector.
- **A truly cold rerank from the store would load about 150 blocks, about 40 MB, per query.** At rerank 10, nearly every one of the 200 reranked vectors sits in a different block, so the cold-equivalent bytes at beam 512 rise from 94 MB to 133 MB. The cold fill pass shows this directly: cold reranks from S3 take 400 ms at beam 128.
- **Noise is larger with parallel scans.** The A/A pair differs by up to ±5% per configuration (B/A 0.96 to 1.05), against ±0.5% in round two. Changes smaller than about 5% now need repeated processes.

### Next candidates

- **Cut request overhead** with a binary leaf list and a breakdown of its 1.4 ms (already in the plan).
- **Make vector-store rerank cheaper:** reuse one blockfile reader, skip the per-vector copy, and batch keys by block. To cut cold bytes, consider smaller vector blocks or ordering vectors within a leaf by expected rerank use.
- **Improve leaf selection.** The walk reaches 95% of true neighbors at beam 512 where an oracle choice of 512 leaves reaches 100%, so better leaf scoring (higher-precision leaf centroids or a rescoring step) is the lever for recall at a fixed beam.
- **Speed up vector-store validation** (900 s) by fetching posting lists in parallel.
- **Known test failures:** five engine expansion tests fail, and they also fail on the accepted commit `4bdd5dc5d`, so they are unrelated to this round.

### What ran

Each change was built on its own branch from `e3ad811b5` (the round-three reader) and benchmarked against that baseline with an A, B, B, A run of four processes: three configurations (beam 128, 512 and 1,024, all rerank 10), all 1,000 queries, vector-store rerank, no local corpus. Two machine pairs ran comparisons concurrently, and each comparison stays within one pair: pair 1 is the original two machines, and pair 2 is a second, identical pair launched for this round (`pairs/pair2.json`). The CPU wake-latency test ran the combined binary with and without the hold, in opposite orders on the two pairs.

- **Scan efficiency** (`perf-scan`, `a573782a0`): reused per-thread buffers, a cached leaf-centroid norm, a per-thread shortlist that skips candidates strictly worse than its running cutoff, and rayon work stealing instead of fixed chunks.
- **Request overhead** (`perf-rpc`, `77f48f7e9`): binary base64 payloads for queries, leaf IDs and results; one write per frame; and a per-request timing breakdown.
- **Vector-store rerank** (`perf-store`, `0a191cc13`): a flat block index built at open, one cache lookup per block, a synchronous path when blocks are cached, and rows lent in place instead of copied.
- **Combined** (`bee07765d`): all three merged on `reader-bench`.
- **CPU wake latency:** a run option (`--hold-cpu-latency 10`) that holds `/dev/cpu_dma_latency` at 10 µs on every machine for the duration of a run. This keeps idle cores out of the C6 sleep state, whose exit latency on these machines is 170 µs. It is released when the run ends.

### Results (B/A total warm latency, 95% interval over queries; IDs identical in every comparison)

| Change | beam 128 | beam 512 | beam 1,024 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scan efficiency | 0.996 (0.988–1.004) | 0.977 (0.972–0.982) | 0.972 (0.967–0.977) |
| Request overhead | 1.024 (1.017–1.032) | 1.006 (1.001–1.012) | 0.976 (0.971–0.980) |
| Vector-store rerank | 0.966 (0.958–0.974) | 0.920 (0.914–0.925) | 0.944 (0.940–0.948) |
| All three combined | 0.902 (0.894–0.909) | 0.892 (0.886–0.897) | 0.911 (0.907–0.916) |
| Wake-latency hold on the combined build, pair 1 | 0.652 (0.645–0.659) | 0.648 (0.643–0.653) | 0.667 (0.663–0.672) |
| Wake-latency hold on the combined build, pair 2 | 0.641 (0.634–0.647) | 0.650 (0.645–0.655) | 0.675 (0.670–0.679) |

- **At the recall target**, beam 512 with rerank 10 reaches recall@10 of 0.952 at 3.09 ms p50 (minimum over two processes) with the hold. That compares with 4.78 ms for the combined code without the hold, 5.33 ms for the round-three reader, and 19.3 ms in round two. A single process with the hold shows 3.36 ms p50 and 4.55 ms p99.
- **CPU per query does not rise with the hold.** At beam 512 it is 13.0 ms against 13.7 ms on the query machine. The hold costs power, not CPU time.
- **Idle-state wakeups were the largest overhead left.** The request-overhead breakdown measured roughly 0.14 ms for each thread handoff. These handoffs are client spawn, owner decode queue, worker wake, and the client waking on its socket, and that cost matches C6's 170 µs exit latency. With the hold, request overhead falls from 1.33 ms to 0.77 ms at beam 512, owner handoffs from 0.31 to 0.08 ms, and network plus wake from 0.60 to 0.26 ms. The peer's leaf scan falls from 2.16 to 1.17 ms, because the scan pool's threads also wake from C6 on every request.
- **The binary payload barely matters on EC2.** Encoding and decoding were never the bottleneck: they took about 0.17 ms in total before the change.
- **The scan change gives 2 to 3%.** The 1-bit scoring kernel is most of the remaining scan cost.

### What this means for production

A latency-sensitive reader fleet should keep its cores out of deep idle states, whether through `/dev/cpu_dma_latency`, the kernel's `intel_idle.max_cstate`, or instance-level settings, or else avoid sleeping threads on the request path (busy-polling or spinning briefly before blocking). The benchmark should state which it uses. Every round-five comparison should run with the hold, so code changes are not measured against wake-up noise.

### Next candidates

- **Spin briefly before blocking** in the scan pool, transport workers and client, which would achieve the same effect without a host setting. Compare it with the hold.
- **Remove the remaining per-request thread spawn** on the query machine (0.04–0.14 ms).
- **Navigation is now 0.74 ms of 3.1 ms.** Parallelizing the 6,905-code leaf-level scoring is the next largest step.
- **Speed up the 1-bit scoring kernel**, the main remaining scan cost.
- **Balance owners.** The peer still scans about 1.4 times as many leaves.


## Phase 0 of the 100B scaling study: FineWeb 1M, 3M and 10M (October 24, 2026)

Phase 0 asks, cheaply and before any 100M build, whether search work at a fixed recall levels off as the corpus grows. It uses the three existing FineWeb indexes, the 1,000 development queries and their exact top-100 answers. Every run is one reader process on the query machine (`i-011ff180f03584f40`) scanning all owners locally, with idle cores held out of deep sleep (`--hold-cpu-latency 10`). The binary is `phase0-6f278224b0e2` (commit `6f278224b`, branch `phase0`), which adds per-level beam caps, recorded leaf IDs, a tree dump, and memory measured right after the routing tree opens. Driver: `phase0-runs.sh`; log: `phase0-runs.log`.

The three indexes are not a controlled ladder. They share the batch schedule (100K, then 1M batches) but come from two writer builds, and the 3M index moved half its subtrees to the second owner at 2M and finished on both owners, while 1M and 10M moved only at the end. The 1M and 3M indexes are format v1 and the 10M runs use the v2 rebuild of the same tree (`rebuilds/v2-10m-c`); both formats score the same codes. Treat the curves as preliminary.

### Leaves needed for a fixed recall grow with corpus size

The grid sweeps 8 beam widths (16 to 2,048 leaves) and 3 rerank depths at recall@10 and recall@100 (`configs/phase0-grid.json`). `frontier.py` takes the cheapest configuration at each recall level and interpolates between grid points; intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over queries.

| Target | 1M leaves | 3M leaves | 10M leaves | Growth exponent, 1M→10M | 10M CPU ms | 10M latency ms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| recall@10 0.90 | 64 (64–67) | 128 (128–128) | 166 (128–256) | 0.41 | 12.1 | 1.74 |
| recall@10 0.95 | 128 (128–149) | 256 (256–310) | 512 (512–609) | 0.60 | 25.9 | 2.80 |
| recall@100 0.90 | 128 (116–128) | 217 (174–256) | 344 (256–479) | 0.43 | 21.7 | 2.78 |
| recall@100 0.95 | 256 (256–256) | 512 (512–512) | 806 (722–1024) | 0.50 | 42.5 | 4.65 |

The leaves needed grow roughly as N^0.4 to N^0.6, which is not a plateau. The grid steps by factors of two, so the interpolated points are coarse, and three points from small trees cannot separate a slowing curve from a steady power law. If the 10M exponent held to 100B, recall@10 0.95 would need 40 to 250 times as many leaves as at 10M; that extrapolation is illustrative only. Full grid points: `p0-frontier.tsv`.

### The loss is in choosing leaves, not in how vectors are grouped

At every size, the true top 100 of a query lie in very few leaves. The best possible 64 leaves would hold 99.8% of them at 1M, 99.4% at 3M and 99.1% at 10M (the `opt R` column), so the grouping does not spread neighbors out as the corpus grows. What grows is the number of leaves navigation must scan to cover those few: at beam 512, the leaves chosen by centroid distance cover 99.8%, 97.8% and 95.3% of the recall@10 neighbors at 1M, 3M and 10M. Above the leaves, all three trees are searched exhaustively at beams of 128 or more, so this loss is entirely leaf ranking.

### Partly searched internal levels lose recall quickly

The level-cap runs limit one internal level to a fixed number of nodes (`configs/phase0-levelcap-*.json`). The share of true neighbors still reachable under the kept nodes:

| Index, level | Keep 2–4% | Keep 6–7% | Keep 12–15% | Keep 24–29% | Keep 48–59% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3M, level 1 (33 nodes) | 0.47 (3%) | 0.62 | 0.76 | 0.88 | 0.96 |
| 10M, level 2 (109 nodes) | 0.55 (2%), 0.68 (4%) | 0.79 | 0.88 | 0.95 | 0.99 |

(recall@10 neighbors; recall@100 is 2–3 points lower.) Reaching 95% at a level takes about 30% of its nodes at 10M. A 100B tree keeps about 2–3% at each of its partly searched internal levels at beam 512. If the needed share stays near 30%, navigation at 100B would need internal beams of hundreds of thousands of nodes; if what matters is an absolute count, it stays cheap. The 100M ladder decides between these, because its second level has about 1,100 nodes.

### Fan-out: a query's leaves are scattered across subtrees

`fanout.py` splits the 10M tree's leaves into M parts by subtree (consecutive in depth-first order, equal posting bytes) or at random, and counts the parts holding each query's chosen leaves (`runs/p0-fanout-10m`, warm pass, `p0-fanout.tsv`). At beam 512, a query's leaves fall under 59.6 of the 109 second-level nodes on average; at beam 128, 23.3.

Subtree placement contacts every part until each part holds fewer leaves than about 60 query beams, and still contacts half the parts at 256 parts. At 10M the regime that matters at 100B, where each machine holds thousands of times the leaves one query scans, is out of reach (2 parts give only 7 times), so these counts bound locality from above rather than predict it.

### Routing-tree memory

After opening the 10M v2 index, the reader holds 7.74 MB of net heap for 7,017 nodes, or 1,103 bytes per node (peak 11.1 MB during open; RSS grows by 33 MB including runtime). That is 0.77 bytes per vector at 768 dimensions: about 77 GB at 100B, and about 0.66 trillion vectors in 512 GB. The 4-bit codes alone are 384 bytes per node, so most of the structure is overhead the plan already lists to remove.

### Exact-centroid leaf ranking: code precision is not the cause

Navigation ranks leaves by distance from the query to each leaf's centroid, using 4-bit centroid codes. To test whether the 4-bit codes cause the growing leaf counts, `--exact-leaf-ranking` (commit `ae5be2555`, binary `phase0-ae5be25554f1`) ranks every leaf of the v1 indexes by exact distance to its float32 centroid and measures the share of each query's true neighbors whose leaves fall inside the top B (runs `p0-exactrank-{1m,3m,10m}`). The 4-bit column is the measured leaf reach from the grid runs; above the leaf level navigation is exhaustive at these beams except at 10M below beam 128.

| Beam | 1m k=10 exact / 4-bit | 3m k=10 exact / 4-bit | 10m k=10 exact / 4-bit | 1m k=100 exact / 4-bit | 3m k=100 exact / 4-bit | 10m k=100 exact / 4-bit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 | 0.783 / 0.774 | 0.738 / 0.725 | 0.718 / 0.688 | 0.728 / 0.721 | 0.677 / 0.664 | 0.645 / 0.617 |
| 64 | 0.912 / 0.906 | 0.874 / 0.869 | 0.843 / 0.839 | 0.883 / 0.879 | 0.835 / 0.830 | 0.796 / 0.791 |
| 128 | 0.956 / 0.951 | 0.919 / 0.916 | 0.891 / 0.890 | 0.938 / 0.934 | 0.893 / 0.888 | 0.856 / 0.852 |
| 512 | 0.999 / 0.998 | 0.978 / 0.978 | 0.955 / 0.953 | 0.997 / 0.997 | 0.971 / 0.969 | 0.939 / 0.937 |
| 2048 | 1.000 / 1.000 | 1.000 / 1.000 | 0.990 / 0.989 | 1.000 / 1.000 | 1.000 / 1.000 | 0.987 / 0.986 |

Exact ranking is at most 3 points better than the 4-bit codes, and under half a point at 10M for beams of 128 or more. Ranking leaves by centroid distance is itself what degrades with corpus size.

The per-query distribution shows where the growth comes from. For each query, the table gives the number of exactly ranked leaves needed to cover its true neighbors:

| Leaves to cover | 1M | 3M | 10M | Growth, 1M→10M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| all of the top 10, p50 query | 48 | 68 | 87 | N^0.26 |
| all of the top 10, p90 query | 270 | 700 | 1616 | N^0.78 |
| all of the top 10, p99 query | 561 | 1539 | 4347 | N^0.89 |
| all of the top 10, mean query | 98 | 223 | 495 | N^0.70 |
| 95% of the top 100, p50 query | 91 | 149 | 220 | N^0.38 |
| 95% of the top 100, p90 query | 276 | 668 | 1585 | N^0.76 |
| 95% of the top 100, p99 query | 459 | 1304 | 3536 | N^0.89 |
| 95% of the top 100, mean query | 121 | 261 | 559 | N^0.66 |

The typical query grows slowly (the median grows about N^0.26 for the top 10), while the hardest tenth grows nearly in proportion to the corpus (about N^0.8). At 1M the hardest queries need most of the 688 leaves, so the index size caps them and the tail exponents are overestimated; the 3M→10M step alone gives about N^0.7 for the p90 query. A fixed beam is set by the hard tail, so the matched-recall cost grows faster than the typical query's need. This points at two remedies to test next: a beam that adapts per query (the reader's distance-ratio `tau` beam, which widens only when many centroids sit at similar distances), and changes to the index that help boundary vectors, such as assigning a vector to more than one leaf.

### Adaptive beam: a distance-ratio beam does not find the hard queries

The reader's adaptive beam keeps every leaf whose centroid distance is within a factor `tau` of the nearest one, bounded by a floor and a cap. The sweep applies it at the leaf level only, with internal levels searched in full (`configs/phase0-tau-*.json`: `tau` 1.15 to 1.8, floors 16, 64 and 128, cap 8,192; binary `phase0-8ff6251651a2`, commit `8ff625165`, which adds per-level beam floors and per-level `tau` to bench configs). Leaves are interpolated along each policy's own cheapest-configuration frontier; intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals.

| Target | Beam | 1M leaves | 3M leaves | 10M leaves | Growth | 10M CPU ms | 10M latency ms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| recall@10 0.90 | fixed | 64 (64–67.18) | 128 (128–128) | 166 (128–256) | N^0.41 | 12.1 | 1.74 |
| recall@10 0.90 | leaf-level tau | 61 (57.34–65.19) | 96 (83.64–115.1) | 148 (127.8–173.8) | N^0.38 | 11.8 | 1.72 |
| recall@10 0.95 | fixed | 128 (128–148.8) | 256 (256–311.9) | 512 (505.6–612.5) | N^0.60 | 25.9 | 2.80 |
| recall@10 0.95 | leaf-level tau | 112 (99.53–133.6) | 238 (185.4–262.6) | 488 (438.5–547.1) | N^0.64 | 24.6 | 2.85 |
| recall@100 0.90 | fixed | 128 (115.4–128) | 217 (173–256) | 344 (256–512) | N^0.43 | 21.6 | 2.78 |
| recall@100 0.90 | leaf-level tau | 81 (76.28–86.8) | 148 (136.9–163.4) | 300 (262.4–353.5) | N^0.57 | 19.6 | 2.75 |
| recall@100 0.95 | fixed | 256 (256–256) | 512 (512–512) | 806 (711.3–1024) | N^0.50 | 42.5 | 4.65 |
| recall@100 0.95 | leaf-level tau | 162 (153.4–171.8) | 372 (349.9–416.9) | 1080 (993.2–1168) | N^0.83 | 50.8 | 5.28 |

At 1M and 3M the adaptive beam reaches the same recall with 5–37% fewer leaves. At 10M the advantage shrinks to 5–13% at three targets and reverses at recall@100 0.95, where it needs 1,080 leaves against 806. At three of the four targets its leaf counts grow as fast as a fixed beam's or faster, up to N^0.83. A query's centroid distance ratios therefore do not identify the hard tail as the index grows, so a smarter beam over the same centroid ranking is not the remedy. The remaining candidates change the index or the ranking signal: assigning boundary vectors to more than one leaf, and ranking leaves with information beyond the centroid, such as each leaf's radius.

## The 100M FineWeb ladder: build, depth limit, placement and the routing stand-in (October 25, 2026)

### The writer's balancing depth limit, and a 100M single-owner build

The first 100M ladder build stalled in long balancing passes: 211 s at 5M, 690 s at 10M, 2,335 s at 21M and 3,187 s at 24M, with under two cores busy and about 30 times the normal splits while adding the usual ~700 leaves. Every balancing job carried a depth, but nothing increased it: reassignments, merges and transfers scheduled their follow-up work at depth 0, so the reference writer's limit (stop chained balancing past depth 4) never applied. Work triggered by moving vectors now runs one level deeper than the job that moved them, and work past depth 4 is dropped for that pass; each pass starts its out-of-threshold nodes again at depth 0, so dropped work is reconsidered after the next batch. Split children and parents overfilled by a split keep their job's depth, as structural refinement does in the reference (commits `7979ebc6b`, `e2dd37908`, `c9d0f4823` on branch `phase0`). The distributed test suite passes apart from the five known endpoint failures and one save-concurrency test with a one-second deadline that fails only under the full suite's parallel load.

A fresh build with the limit (binary `ladder-writer-c9d0f48238df`; one owner builds every row, 16 balance workers, checkpoints at 1, 2, 3, 5 and every 10M) reached 100M in about 100 minutes of construction. All 100 balancing passes stayed between 0.8 and 28.6 s (median 19.9 s), growing slowly with the tree; the limit dropped 2,124 jobs in total, in 41 of the 100 passes, at most 158 in one pass. Per-pass detail: `ladder2-build-passes.txt`.

| Batch ending at | Balance time | Splits | Jobs dropped at depth limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10M | 12.1 s | 726 | 143 |
| 30M | 15.2 s | 758 | 0 |
| 50M | 19.7 s | 751 | 125 |
| 70M | 23.5 s | 799 | 0 |
| 100M | 26.2 s | 727 | 94 |

The input is the first 100M rows of the pinned FineWeb manifest, exported to one float32 file in 14 minutes (`export-fineweb.py`); its first 10M rows hash identically to the existing 10M input. Exact top-100 answers for the 1,000 development and 10,000 test queries at all 14 ladder sizes come from one scan of the corpus per query shard (32 minutes); the development answers at 10M match the existing ones for all 1,000 queries.

### Saving: single-owner generations, hash receipts and a port race

A generation saved without placement (every vector on owner 1) failed fresh-reader validation with "missing saved child": before placement, splits under the root never republish the shared view, so the save wrote a stale root. The save now writes the owner's current root when the global root is the owner's unit root (commit `775ba85d5`), and skips the two-owner share gate for an unplaced save (`28b783049`). A single-owner 1M save validates with 1,000,000 vectors on owner 1 and none on owner 2.

Each save spent about 14 of its 14.5 minutes hashing the 307 GB input three times (two writer processes and the validating reader). With `SPANN_INPUT_RECEIPT_DIR`, writer processes reuse the reader's corpus hash receipt (`c1eef3ca5`); a 1M save then takes about a minute. Saves overlapping a still-exiting second owner failed with "address already in use"; the save script now waits for its second owner to exit. Saving the 100M size with both owners' full-vector stores exceeded the writer's 30-minute save budget; the budget is now configurable (`SPANN_SAVE_OPERATION_SECONDS`, `53a26ad03`). The machine-count experiment reads a single-owner 100M save with its full-vector store, made with a 3-hour budget (`/data/ladder2/store-100000000`, prefix `sha256/ladder100m-v3-store`).

The full-vector store is written by one thread, one 256 MiB chunk upload at a time. The 100M single-owner save with its store uploaded at about 36 MB/s, so its 307 GB take about 2.4 hours. The writer now cuts an owner's leaves into contiguous ranges of about equal vector count and writes each range to its own blockfile on its own thread, reading a leaf's vectors as it reaches the leaf instead of collecting every vector first (commits `8df9c5d0b`, `997b011be`). A reader joins the segments' block indexes into one, and single-blockfile stores stay readable. The validating reader compares stored vectors with the corpus on 32 threads. Writing 6 GB to S3 from an r6i.16xlarge (pair c) measured:

| writers | MB/s, run 1 | MB/s, run 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 76 (3 GB) | - |
| 4 | 305 | 306 |
| 8 | 525 (3 GB) | - |
| 16 | 845 | 856 |
| 32 | 867 | failed: 429 SlowDown |
| 64 | failed: S3 error (3 GB) | - |

Every segment writes under the owner's one S3 prefix, so 32 or more writers sometimes exceed S3's request rate for that prefix. The default is 16 writers (`SPANN_VECTOR_STORE_WRITERS`), and a failed segment is written again from its first leaf, up to four attempts. At about 850 MB/s a 307 GB store takes about 6 minutes; this is an estimate from the 6 GB runs, since no full-size store has been written this way yet. The 100M store save that started at 13:10 UTC uses the single writer. A 1M single-owner save with the parallel writer passed fresh-reader validation: the store has the segmented layout (16 segments; the first holds 63,893 rows), every one of its 1,000,000 vectors matches the corpus bit for bit, and the whole save and validation took 46 s, 5.9 s of it verifying the store (`/data/vector-store-check.sh`, output `/data/ladder2/vstore-check-1000000`). The parallel reader also validated the 100M store written by the single writer in 1,266 s: 313 s for the vector store and 927 s for membership and code checks, which still run on one thread. `ladder-save.sh` now defaults to the parallel writer and its reader.

### Read-time placement

`--parts M` makes every reader process split the leaves into M parts when it opens an index: leaves in depth-first order, so subtrees stay together, cut into runs of nearly equal posting bytes. Leaves route to their part instead of their saved owner, a process serving some parts opens only the vector stores holding their leaves and keeps only those leaves' blocks in each store's block index, and serve mode accepts several parts (`eed153a67`, tests `4c9c32f3c`). Validation on the 1M FineWeb index (two saved owners), 1,000 development queries:

- Without rerank, returned IDs are identical for 1, 2 and 4 parts and for the saved-owner routing, for all 1,000 queries at recall@10 (beam 128) and recall@100 (beam 512). Each part returns its best k by 1-bit score, so the merge cannot depend on the part count.
- With rerank, each part reranks its own shortlist, so more parts rerank more candidates: recall@100 at beam 512, rerank 4 is 0.980, 0.991 and 0.994 for 1, 2 and 4 parts.
- Across two machines (parts 1–2 on the query machine, 3–4 served by the peer, `--parts 4`), IDs and distances are identical to the one-process 4-part run for all 1,000 queries in every configuration, rerank included. Both machines computed the same placement (173, 170, 167 and 178 leaves).
- The single-owner 1M generation read with 1, 2 and 4 parts returns identical IDs without rerank for all 1,000 queries (parts of 162, 177, 169 and 179 leaves).

### Routing stand-in: navigation at the depth of a 100B tree

`routing_standin.py` treats N real FineWeb vectors as leaf centroids and groups them by top-down hierarchical k-means at fan-out 63, giving a tree with the depth and level widths of a real tree with N leaves (about 1,420 vectors per leaf). Navigation follows the reader's beam over exact centroid distances. The truth for a query is its 10 nearest stand-in leaves, so this measures how well hierarchical navigation finds the nearest leaf centroids, separate from how vectors are grouped. Reach is the share of those 10 leaves that navigation keeps, with leaf beam 512 (results: `standin/report-*.json`).

| Stand-in leaves (tree of) | Level widths below the root | Internal beam 512 | 2,048 | 8,192 | Parts contacted of 10 / 50 / 200 (beam 512, subtree placement) | Queries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 70K (about 100M vectors) | 18 / 1109 / 70000 | 0.991 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 9.8 / 38.0 / 93.9 | 1000 |
| 700K (1B) | 3 / 176 / 11110 / 700000 | 0.920 | 0.979 | 0.999 | 8.9 / 26.6 / 47.6 | 1000 |
| 7M (10B) | 28 / 1763 / 111138 / 7000000 | 0.846 | 0.927 | 0.978 | 7.1 / 15.4 / 29.3 | 300 |
| 70M (100B) | 4 / 281 / 17629 / 1111086 / 70000000 | 0.828 | 0.892 | 0.954 | 6.8 / 14.4 / 20.4 | 200 |

At the 100M shape a beam of 512 at internal levels keeps 99% of the nearest leaves; at the 100B shape it keeps 83%, and 8,192 keeps 95%. The internal beam needed for about 95% grows roughly fourfold per tenfold growth in leaves, the same N^0.5–0.6 pattern the leaf level showed in Phase 0. An internal beam of 8,192 at 100B scores about one million centroid codes per query (all 17,629 nodes of the third level, then 8,192 × 63 children at each of the two levels below), about 1.4 times the 760,000 posting codes a 512-leaf scan scores. Fan-out stays well below the number of parts: with 200 parts, a query's 512 leaves fall in about 20 of them at the 100B shape.

### Growth ladder: FineWeb 1M to 100M from one build

Every size comes from the one depth-limited build above, saved from its checkpoint and benchmarked on the builder (r6i.32xlarge) with one reader process pinned to 28 cores of one socket, all owners local, rerank from the memory-mapped corpus, CPU wake latency held at 10 µs, and the 1,000 development queries with exact answers for that size (driver `bench-ladder.sh`; binary `ladder-reader-1633b24ad2a7`, and `ladder-reader-c1eef3ca52c6` with `--parts 2` for 80M and 100M). Sizes up to 70M and 90M were saved with two owners. 80M was saved with one owner because its placement failed with an encoding error ("cannot encode JSON frame"; cause not yet confirmed, see the placement-message entry in `CURRENT-PLAN.md`). 100M was saved with one owner because its two-owner placement finished but its save failed, first on the save deadline and then on leftover S3 objects from that attempt. Both are read as two subtree parts, so every size reranks two shortlists. The grid is 8 beams × 3 rerank depths at recall@10 and recall@100 (`configs/phase0-grid.json`), plus beams of 4,096 and 8,192 from 10M up (`configs/ladder-grid-wide.json`). These benchmarks shared the machine with the build, the saves and each other, so their latency and CPU times are noisy; recall and work counts are not affected. The latency and CPU figures in this section therefore come from quiet reruns: the 1M, 10M, 30M and 100M grids, the 10M, 30M and 100M wide beams and the 100M level-cap sweep, run one at a time on the otherwise idle builder with the same inputs, binaries and arguments (driver `quiet-ladder.sh`, labels `lad2q-*`). The reruns return the same IDs and do the same work as the first runs for every query. At each run's median configuration, their median latency is 0–7% lower than the first runs'; the worst case is a 1M configuration that ran 2.9× slower the first time. Run directories are on the builder under `reader-dev/runs/lad2-*`; summaries and run receipts are copied to `runs-ladder2/`.

Recall at a fixed beam keeps falling to 100M, but more slowly with size: at 512 leaves recall@10 loses about 0.013 per doubling of the corpus from 1M to 10M and about 0.010 per doubling from 10M to 100M (0.954 to 0.922). The second internal level is first searched partly at 50M (512 of 535 nodes) and still keeps over 99.5% of the neighbors there at 100M.

The leaves needed grow roughly as N^0.3 to N^0.55 from 10M to 100M depending on the target, against N^0.4 to N^0.6 from 1M to 10M in Phase 0. The grid steps by factors of two, so flat stretches (for example 2,048 at 30M–80M for recall@100 0.95) are grid artifacts; the fixed-beam table is the cleaner signal. Nothing here plateaus.

**Cost at matched recall:**

| Target | Metric | 1M | 10M | 30M | 100M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| recall@10 0.95 | CPU ms | 7.9 | 25.5 | 44.0 | 61.4 |
| recall@10 0.95 | latency ms | 0.76 | 2.7 | 5.9 | 12.9 |
| recall@100 0.95 | CPU ms | 17.6 | 43.3 | 93.8 | 119.6 |
| recall@100 0.95 | latency ms | 1.7 | 4.7 | 10.2 | 20.2 |

Costs are from the quiet reruns, interpolated between the grid configurations that bracket the target (`lad2q-frontier.tsv` has the bootstrap intervals). The 1M recall@10 cost is lower than the first runs suggested (7.9 against 11.5 ms of CPU) because noise had made the cheapest configuration, beam 128 with rerank 10, look more expensive than beam 256 with rerank 4.

At 10M the same level (109 nodes) needed about 32 kept nodes (29%) for 95% reach; at 100M it needs about 90 (8%). Neither the share nor the count of nodes stays constant: the count needed grows about N^0.45, consistent with the routing stand-in. The caps also cut latency: with 2,048 leaves and the second level capped at 128 nodes, recall@10 is 0.952 at 8.4 ms, against 0.947 at 12.1 ms for an uncapped beam of 1,024, because the leaf level then scores about 8,000 centroids instead of 69,000.

**Fan-out at 100M.** At 512 leaves a query's leaves fall under 12.3 of the 16 first-level nodes and 91 of the 1,096 second-level nodes. Splitting the leaves by subtree into M parts (`lad2-fanout-100m.tsv`):

**Routing-tree memory at 100M:** 75.4 MB of net heap for 69,870 nodes after open, 1,080 bytes per node, the same per-node cost as at 10M; 0.75 bytes per vector, or about 75 GB at 100B.

## Machine count: one 100M index served from 1, 2, 4 and 8 machines (October 25, 2026)

This experiment serves the same 100M FineWeb index from 1, 2, 4 and 8 identical machines and measures what changes: recall, single-query latency, throughput under concurrent load, and the total work per query. Every reader process splits the index into M parts when it opens it (read-time placement, `--parts M`: leaves in depth-first order, cut into runs of equal posting bytes). One machine, the query machine, navigates every query's routing tree, scans its own part and sends one scan request to each other part's machine. Each part ranks its own candidates by 1-bit score and reranks its own shortlist with full vectors, so a query with M parts reranks up to M times as many vectors.

### What ran

- **Index:** the 100M ladder size, saved with one owner and its full-vector store in S3 (generation `gen-404040`, prefix `sha256/ladder100m-v3-store`). Posting lists and full vectors are read from S3 and cached in memory; no machine holds a copy of the corpus.
- **Machines:** r6i.4xlarge (16 vCPUs, 128 GB), one per part, so the total hardware grows with M. Placement cuts parts of equal posting bytes; their leaf counts are within 1.3% of each other (34,386 and 34,371 at M=2; 8,534 to 8,640 at M=8).
- **Caches per process:** 64 GiB posting cache (100M postings occupy about 12 GB) and a vector-store block cache of 280,000 blocks: up to 147 GB if every block were full size, about 62 GB at the measured 220 KB average (see "Vector cache size" below).
- **Queries and passes:** the 1,000 development queries with exact answers at 100M. Each configuration runs a 32-thread pass, then a one-at-a-time pass for latency, then a second 32-thread pass for throughput on warm caches. The first pass of a configuration starts with the caches left by the configurations before it, so only the first configuration starts fully cold.
- **Configurations:** recall@10 at beam 512 without and with rerank (×10), recall@10 at beam 2,048 with rerank, and recall@100 at beams 1,024 and 4,096 with rerank ×4.
- **Binary:** `fleet-reader-fa803339b6e5` (commit `fa803339b`), driver `fleet.py`. The driver raises each process's open-file limit (see "Fixes needed to run it").

### Results

Warm figures come from the one-at-a-time pass. "CPU ms per query" adds the query machine's CPU to every serving machine's CPU for the same query. Throughput is 1,000 queries over the second 32-thread pass's wall time; the first-pass column is the same for each configuration's first 32-thread pass, which starts with the caches left by earlier configurations. Peak RSS is the query machine's process peak through that configuration.

**Without rerank, recall does not depend on the machine count; with rerank it rises slightly.** Without rerank every machine count returns identical recall (0.7347), as read-time placement guarantees. With rerank, each part keeps and reranks its own shortlist, so the union of the parts' shortlists contains the one-part shortlist and more parts rerank more candidates. Recall@100 at beam 4,096 is 0.9606, 0.9642, 0.9659 and 0.9667 at 1, 2, 4 and 8 machines; no query's recall drops as M grows. Nearly every recall@100 miss is a tie beyond the listed exact answers that the run cannot resolve without the corpus, so recall@100 is a lower bound.

**Single-query latency has two floors that more machines do not lower: navigation and the slowest part.** Warm median latency for recall@100 at beam 4,096 falls from 30.7 ms on one machine to 20.4 ms on eight, and stays at about 7 ms for beam 512 at every M.

- *Navigation.* The query machine walks the routing tree for every query on one thread: 4.3–4.6 ms at beam 512, 8.6–9.0 ms at beam 1,024 and about 12 ms at beams 2,048 and 4,096, the same at every M. At beams of 2,048 and above it scores every one of the 69,869 routing nodes (1,113 internal expansions, all 68,757 leaf centroids), at about 175 ns per distance. At eight machines navigation is 59% of the latency at beam 4,096. Navigation runs on one thread while the scan uses 16, so spreading navigation across the query machine's cores would lower this floor without adding machines.
- *The slowest part.* A query waits for its slowest part. At eight machines and beam 4,096 the median remote request takes 4.4 ms, but the median of each query's slowest remote request is 7.1 ms: navigation (12.1 ms) plus the slowest part (7.1 ms) plus the merge accounts for the 20.4 ms. Parts are balanced overall (leaf counts within 1.3%) but not per query: at eight subtree parts the busiest part holds on average 43% of a query's leaves at beam 512 and 38% at beam 1,024, against 12.5% for an even split (fan-out analysis, `lad2-fanout-100m.tsv`).
- *Request overhead.* Each remote request adds a median 0.5–1.0 ms (encoding, transfer and wake-up) on a warm path.

**The 32-thread pass measures throughput at 32 queries in flight, and under that load most of a query's time goes to starting threads on the query machine.** Recall@100 at beam 1,024 serves 192, 315, 427 and 425 queries per second at 1, 2, 4 and 8 machines; beam 4,096 serves 63, 113, 181 and 217. From four to eight machines, beam 512 loses throughput (814 to 723 without rerank) while beams 2,048 and 4,096 gain 16% and 20%. Throughput follows from latency at fixed concurrency: 32 queries in flight at the pass's 74 ms median give about 430 queries per second, and the run measured 425. The latency under load comes mostly from one mechanism:

- The query machine starts a new OS thread for every remote part of every query (`std::thread::scope` in `OwnerQuery::query`). One at a time, the slowest of these threads starts within 0.1–0.2 ms. In the 32-thread pass at eight machines it starts 16 ms late at beam 512 and 26 ms late at beam 1,024, out of medians of 44 and 74 ms; navigation also slows from 4.3 to 8.4 ms and from 8.7 to 18.3 ms. The slowest remote request itself takes 3.8 and 9.7 ms. On the serving machines, worker wake-up and decode queueing stay near 0.03 ms.
- The data cannot separate two causes: a full CPU run queue on the query machine, or the kernel's cost of creating threads in a process with 25–65 GB mapped. The query machine's warm-pass CPU (24.8 ms per query at eight machines, about 10.5 vCPUs at 425 queries per second) is lower than at four machines (29.3 ms, about 12.5 vCPUs), so a fixed CPU budget does not explain the plateau by itself. The bench does not record process CPU during 32-thread passes.
- What would settle it: record the query machine's user and system CPU and run-queue length during the 32-thread pass; sweep the client thread count (16, 32, 64); and replace per-request threads with persistent per-remote workers. The last is also the likely fix. In this setup one machine coordinates every query; a deployment that spreads coordination across machines would also spread this cost, but these runs do not measure that.

**Total CPU per query grows with the machine count, mostly because the same vectors cost more to scan in smaller pieces.** For recall@100 at beam 1,024, CPU summed over all machines rises from 77 to 118 ms per query from one machine to eight; recall@10 at beam 512 without rerank rises from 36.5 to 56.9 ms. The scan of the same 761,545 vectors (recall@10, beam 512) takes 2.1 ms summed over parts on one machine and 4.2 ms over eight. Rerank time grows from 0.9 to 5.8 ms summed over parts for recall@100 at beam 1,024 (400 to 3,177 vectors reranked), a small share of the 41 ms growth. Configurations with very different rerank volumes grow by similar amounts (41 ms at recall@100 beam 1,024; 39 ms at recall@10 beam 2,048). The CPU figure counts the 16-thread scan pool's time, so part of the growth may be pool threads waiting on small per-part requests rather than useful work. A shortlist chosen across parts before rerank would cut rerank volume, but it would also remove the recall gain above and add a round trip.

**A query contacts almost every part.** At eight parts a query contacts 7.7 parts on average at beam 512 and 7.9–8.0 at beams 1,024 and above, exactly as the ladder's fan-out analysis predicted for eight subtree parts (7.71 and 7.94). A query's leaves are spread across subtrees, so subtree placement does not confine a query to a few machines at this size.

**The first pass of a configuration is limited by S3 reads and mostly improves with machines.** The first configuration's first pass, with every posting list fetched from S3, serves 18, 32, 55 and 61 queries per second at 1, 2, 4 and 8 machines. Recall@100 at beam 1,024, whose first pass loads the full vectors for rerank from S3, serves 32, 36, 58 and 65. The gain is not monotonic everywhere: recall@10 at beam 512 with rerank serves 70 at four machines and 59 at eight.

**Memory per machine falls with M.** The query machine's peak RSS through the last configuration is 69, 57, 43 and 29 GB at 1, 2, 4 and 8 machines; the vector cache is most of it.

### Vector cache size: rerank from the vector store needs the warm pass's blocks in cache

The vector store keeps full vectors in blocks of up to 512 KiB, ordered by leaf; stored blocks average about 220 KB. Rerank loads the whole block that holds each vector. A warm recall@100 query reranks 400 vectors from about 230 blocks, so it touches about 50 MB of blocks to use 1.2 MB of vectors. The block cache counts blocks: its capacity is the byte budget divided by the 512 KiB maximum block size. The cache evicts the least recently used block, and the warm pass repeats the 1,000 queries in the same order, so if the pass's distinct blocks exceed the capacity, almost nothing is still cached when it is needed again.

A first 1-machine run with a 32 GiB budget (65,536 blocks) missed on nearly every block: each warm recall@100 query loaded about 50 MB from S3, and warm median latency was 719 ms at beam 1,024 and 758 ms at beam 4,096 (table "fleet-100m-1machines, 32 GiB vector cache" below; that run used the earlier binary `placement-4c9c32f3c708`, which predates the retries and the multi-segment vector-store reader; the store it read has one segment, so its rerank reads the same blocks). With 280,000 blocks the same queries take 15.2 and 30.7 ms and load nothing from S3. The warm pass touches about 230,000 blocks, but some are shared between queries, so the runs show only that its distinct blocks number more than 65,536 and at most 280,000. The recall@10 configurations touch about 70 blocks per query; in the 32 GiB run their warm passes loaded almost nothing (beam 2,048 loaded 0.6 MB per query).

The closest comparison with a memory-mapped corpus is the quiet ladder rerun at beam 1,024: 12.7 ms on an r6i.32xlarge, reading the index as two parts in one process (800 vectors reranked, recall 0.9199). The fleet's two-machine run reranks the same 800 vectors and reaches 14.5 ms (recall 0.9197).

On a cold cache the block-sized reads remain: each block a query touches costs about 220 KB from S3, about 50 MB for a recall@100 query. Storing full vectors by vector ID instead of by leaf is listed in `CURRENT-PLAN.md` as a follow-up.

### Fixes needed to run it

- **Open-file limit.** Rerank opens many S3 connections at once. At the SSH session's default soft limit of 1,024 open files, the S3 client fails to connect ("dispatch failure") and a serving machine's listener stops on its first failed `accept()`, after which the query machine gets "connection refused". In the failed attempt, a serving machine's log (`serve-2.log` on m2) shows "Too many open files (os error 24)"; it was read on the machine and not copied. Each process now raises its soft limit to the hard limit (1,048,576) before starting.
- **Retries.** Block loads and remote scans are reads, so the reader retries them: up to 4 attempts per block load and 3 per remote scan, each logged (`fa803339b`). The query machine logged no retries in the final runs; the serving machines' logs were not collected.
- **Validation of the 100M generation.** The store save wrote its generation at 15:20 UTC, but its serial fresh-reader validation used about half a core (`ps`) and was stopped. The parallel reader (`reader-ondemand-997b011beac6`, 32 verify threads) then validated it after the quiet ladder rerun: status `durable_reader_validated` in 1,263 s (exact membership of 100,000,000 rows and recomputed centroid and posting codes 927 s; vector-store checksums 313 s; peak RSS 15.3 GB). The record is `/data/ladder2/store-100000000/owner1/durable-validation-997b.json` on the builder.

Outputs of the failed attempts are kept: `runs/fleet-attempt1` (old binary, 32 GiB vector cache, remote rerank failed at M ≥ 2), `runs/fleet-attempt3` (open-file limit, remote rerank failed at M ≥ 2).

### Run tables

The two 32-thread passes of each configuration appear as `cold` and `cold#2`. In 32-thread passes the `vec store MB`, `vec blocks` and `cold-equiv MB` columns read process-wide counters before and after each query, so they include other concurrent queries' loads and are not per-query figures.

## Machine count with persistent remote workers and parallel navigation (October 26, 2026)

This rerun repeats the machine-count experiment above with two changes to the query machine and with CPU recorded during every pass. Everything else is the same: the same 100M index, machines, caches, queries, passes and configurations.

- **Persistent remote workers.** Each remote part has a fixed pool of 64 request threads on the query machine (`--remote-workers`, at least `--cold-threads`). A query hands each remote part's request to a waiting thread and scans its local part meanwhile, instead of starting a new thread per remote part per query.
- **Parallel navigation.** When a level of the routing walk expands 16 or more internal nodes, their children are scored in runs of 16 on rayon's global pool (16 threads on an r6i.4xlarge) and joined in order, so scores, candidate order and beam selection are unchanged.
- **CPU recording.** Each pass records the bench process's user and system CPU, cores busy on average, and voluntary and involuntary context switches (`process_cpu` in `summary.json`). A sampler on every machine logs the aggregate `/proc/stat` CPU line and the number of runnable threads once a second (`cpu-<machine>.log` in each run directory).
- **Binary:** `fleet-reader-df4932e9fa49` (commit `df4932e9f`). "Before" is the run above (`fleet-reader-fa803339b6e5`, outputs now in `runs/fleet-fa803339b`).

### Results

Both binaries return identical IDs and distances for all 1,000 queries in the one-at-a-time pass, in all 20 combinations of configuration and machine count (`fleet_compare.py`). "Slowest remote part's wait" is the median, over the second 32-thread pass, of each query's longest wait on the query machine before a thread started its remote request. "Cores busy" is the bench process's CPU over the second 32-thread pass divided by its wall time.

**Single-query latency falls by 15–29% at every machine count, mostly by about a quarter, because navigation is about 40% faster.** Navigation takes 2.7–2.9 ms at beam 512 (4.3–4.6 before), 4.9–5.3 ms at beam 1,024 (8.6–9.0) and 7.4–7.7 ms at beams 2,048 and 4,096 (11.9–12.4). Recall@100 at beam 4,096 now answers in 26.1 ms on one machine and 15.6 ms on eight; recall@10 at beam 512 in 4.8–5.9 ms. Navigation gets 1.6 times faster on 16 threads, not 16 times: the beam selection over all scored children and the hand-off to the pool stay on the query's thread. At eight machines navigation is still 48% of the latency at beam 4,096.

**Under load the remote request threads no longer wait to start.** At eight machines the slowest remote part's wait falls from 16–50 ms to 0.7–2.6 ms; at four machines from 7–21 ms to 0.3–1.0 ms.

**The query machine's CPU is now the measured limit on throughput.** In every second 32-thread pass, at every machine count, the bench process keeps 13.6–15.8 of the query machine's 16 vCPUs busy, and the per-second sampler shows 16–34 runnable threads on it. Serving machines keep 4.6–13.5 vCPUs busy. The bench process is preempted 25,000–220,000 times a second (involuntary context switches). The 32-thread pass therefore measures how many queries one query machine can navigate, scan and merge per second; the run above could not separate this from thread start-up, and these runs show both were present.

**Throughput rises at eight machines and falls slightly at one and two.** At eight machines the 32-thread pass serves 936 queries per second at recall@10 beam 512 (723 before), 436 at recall@100 beam 1,024 (425) and 235 at beam 4,096 (217); its median latency falls to 29, 71 and 133 ms. At one and two machines throughput falls by 2–12%, and at four machines it is unchanged except recall@100 at beam 1,024 (427 to 377). The cause is CPU: parallel navigation costs more CPU than sequential navigation. One query at a time, the query machine's CPU per query rises from 36.5 to 42.2 ms on one machine and from 13.2 to 18.1 ms on eight, about 5 ms of pool dispatch and idle pool threads spinning. On a query machine that is already full, that CPU comes out of other queries, and navigation in the second 32-thread pass takes 16–63 ms instead of 8–40 ms.

**What this means.** With one machine coordinating every query, throughput is bounded by that machine's CPU, and navigation is the largest share of its per-query work. Two directions follow. Parallel navigation should run only when the query machine has idle cores, for example sequentially once more queries are in flight than it has cores. And coordination should be spread so that each machine navigates and merges its own share of queries, which these runs do not measure.

### Measurement notes

- Per-query `cpu_ms` in one-at-a-time passes is whole-process CPU over the query, so it now includes the navigation pool's CPU, idle spinning included; it is about 5 ms higher than before for the same work.
- The machine sampler has one-second resolution. Second 32-thread passes that finish in about a second (most recall@10 passes at four and eight machines) have fewer than two samples on some machines, and `fleet_compare.py` reports no figure for them.
- The query machine logged no retries and no errors; the serving machines' logs were not collected.

### Run tables

The two 32-thread passes of each configuration appear as `cold` and `cold#2`. In 32-thread passes the `vec store MB`, `vec blocks` and `cold-equiv MB` columns read process-wide counters before and after each query, so they include other concurrent queries' loads. The `req spawn` column is now the wait for a persistent request thread.

## Machine count with navigation parallel only on idle cores (October 26, 2026)

This rerun repeats the machine-count experiment with one more change to the query machine: navigation runs in parallel only when the machine has idle cores. Each query counts the queries in flight in its process, itself included, when it starts. With fewer in flight than the process has cores (16 on an r6i.4xlarge), it scores wide levels on rayon's pool as in the previous section; otherwise it scores every level on its own thread. Both modes return identical leaves. Each query record notes the count and the mode (`queries_in_flight`, `navigation_parallel`). Everything else is unchanged: index, machines, caches, queries, passes, configurations, persistent remote workers and CPU recording.

The table compares three readers:

- **A** starts a thread per remote request and navigates on the query's thread (`fleet-reader-fa803339b6e5`, `runs/fleet-fa803339b`).
- **B** uses persistent remote workers and always navigates in parallel (`fleet-reader-df4932e9fa49`, `runs/fleet-df4932e9f`).
- **C** uses persistent remote workers and navigates in parallel only on idle cores (`fleet-reader-8410e90190ce`, commit `8410e9019`, the run directories `runs/fleet-100m-{M}machines`).

### Results

All three readers return identical IDs and distances for all 1,000 queries in the one-at-a-time pass, in all 20 combinations of configuration and machine count (`fleet_compare.py`). C navigated in parallel for every one-at-a-time query and for 1% of the queries in the second 32-thread pass, which started while the pass was filling to 32 queries. "Preemptions" are the bench process's involuntary context switches; the per-pass CPU record that counts them exists only for B and C.

**One query at a time, C is nearly as fast as B.** Its warm median latency is between 1.6% below and 6.2% above B's, and 14–30% below A's: recall@10 at beam 512 answers in 5.0–6.2 ms and recall@100 at beam 4,096 in 26.5 ms on one machine and 15.6 ms on eight.

**At 32 queries in flight, C has the highest throughput at four and eight machines, and matches A at one and two.** At eight machines C serves 1,098 queries per second at recall@10 beam 512 (A 723, B 936), 531 at recall@100 beam 1,024 (A 425, B 436) and 276 at beam 4,096 (A 217, B 235), with median latency 24.5, 53.5 and 113.6 ms. At four machines it serves 923, 432 and 187 (A 814, 427, 181). At one and two machines it is within 4% of A in every configuration, where B was 2–12% below A. Two effects add up at eight machines: persistent workers remove the thread start-up wait that limited A, and sequential navigation under load avoids the CPU that B's parallel navigation took from other queries. The query machine is preempted 1.7–3.4 times less often than with B (at eight machines, 131,626 against 220,222 times a second at beam 512).

**The query machine is still the limit.** In every second 32-thread pass C keeps 14.9–15.8 of the query machine's 16 vCPUs busy, with 12–38 runnable threads, while serving machines keep 5.7–13.8 busy. Throughput at 32 queries in flight is therefore what one query machine can navigate, scan and merge per second. A deployment that spreads query coordination across machines would raise it; these runs do not measure that.

### Run tables

The two 32-thread passes of each configuration appear as `cold` and `cold#2`. In 32-thread passes the `vec store MB`, `vec blocks` and `cold-equiv MB` columns read process-wide counters before and after each query, so they include other concurrent queries' loads. The `req spawn` column is the wait for a persistent request thread.

## Every machine coordinates queries (October 26, 2026)

The machine-count experiments above route every query through one query machine, so their throughput measures what one machine can navigate and merge. This experiment spreads coordination: on M machines, every machine serves its own part and also runs its own stream of queries, scanning its own part locally and sending one scan request to each other machine. It measures the throughput of the whole fleet when every machine is loaded.

### What ran

- **Index, machines, caches and configurations:** as in the machine-count experiment above. The reader is `fleet-reader-8366bca9ace4` (cited commit `8366bca9a`, published as `a543fd917`), which adds the pass barrier and load pass below to the idle-core navigation reader.
- **Each machine:** one server for its part (`--scan-handlers 256`, since a server answers up to (M − 1) × 32 requests at once) and one bench over all 1,000 development queries with 32 threads. Machine j starts its query list at query (j − 1) × 1,000 / M, so machines do not walk the same queries in step.
- **Passes:** each configuration runs a 32-thread pass, a one-at-a-time pass and a load pass, a 32-thread pass over the queries repeated 10 times. A pass barrier starts each pass on every machine at the same moment: each bench announces it is ready, and the driver writes a start time 10 s ahead on m1's clock (`--pass-barrier`). All eight machines' clocks were within 5 µs of NTP time, and passes started within 0.1 ms of each other.
- **Aggregate throughput:** the queries, on all machines, that started and finished inside the load pass's common window (the latest machine's start to the earliest machine's finish), divided by the window's length (`spread_analyze.py`).
- **Driver:** `fleet.py spread`; outputs in `runs/fleet-spread-{M}machines/m{j}`.

### Results

"Load" latency is over the load pass's queries inside the common window. "Warm" is the one-at-a-time pass, which now runs on every machine at once, so each server also answers M − 1 other query streams. "Identical IDs" compares every one-at-a-time query on every machine with the single-coordinator run at the same M. "Machine cores busy" and "runnable threads" are the range over machines in the common window, from each machine's per-second CPU sampler.

**Aggregate throughput grows with machines, at 54–62% efficiency on eight.** Relative to one machine, two machines serve 1.8–1.9 times as many queries per second, four serve 2.8–3.3 times and eight serve 4.3–5.0 times. Recall@10 at beam 512 without rerank grows from 408 to 725, 1,227 and 2,046 queries per second; recall@100 at beam 1,024 from 192 to 349, 538 and 823; recall@100 at beam 4,096 from 63 to 119, 210 and 306. At eight machines this is 1.9, 1.5 and 1.1 times the single-coordinator throughput above (1,098, 531 and 276 queries per second at 32 queries in flight), which shows the single query machine was the limit there.

**The hottest part's machine sets the limit.** Placement cuts parts of equal posting bytes, but queries do not scan the parts equally. At four machines, part 4 receives 28.9% of the scanned vectors (25% would be even), and in the common window its machine keeps 15.6 of 16 cores busy while the others keep 11–13 busy. At eight machines and recall@100 beam 4,096, part 5 receives 15.7% (12.5% would be even), and its machine runs at 15.9 cores while the others run at 10–12. Every query waits for its slowest part, so each machine's queries queue behind the hot part's server. The machine that hosts the hot part scans it locally and finishes its own 10,000 queries 1.3–2.9 times sooner than the others: at eight machines and beam 4,096, m5 finishes in 82 s and the others in 178–236 s. The queueing also shows in tail latency: at eight machines the load pass's p99 is 0.9–9.0 s, against median 44–283 ms.

**Results do not change.** Every one-at-a-time query on every machine returns the same IDs and distances as the single-coordinator run at the same machine count.

**One query at a time gets slower when every machine is querying.** At eight machines the one-at-a-time median is 7.0 ms at recall@10 beam 512 without rerank and 32.7 ms at recall@100 beam 4,096, against 5.0 and 15.6 ms with a single coordinator, because each server now also answers seven other query streams.

**What this means.** Spreading coordination removes the single-query-machine limit, and the next limit is load balance across parts. Two directions follow: place leaves by measured scan load rather than by posting bytes, and serve hot parts from more than one machine.

### Measurement notes

- Server-side CPU and heap fields in query records (`remote_cpu_seconds`, `remote_heap_peak_bytes`) are process-wide, so with several query streams they include other streams' requests.
- Load-pass query records are kept with timing and recall fields only (`slim.py` in `fleet.py`); per-query work columns in the run tables are empty for load passes.
- At eight machines, copying results back failed for m4–m8 on the first try because the local disk was full; they were copied again from the stopped machines' disks. Every bench exited with status 0.

### Run tables

Each machine's table, with the 32-thread pass as `cold`, the one-at-a-time pass as `warm` and the load pass as `load`. In 32-thread passes the `vec store MB`, `vec blocks` and `cold-equiv MB` columns read process-wide counters, so they include other concurrent queries' loads.
